newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Deng's death puts hold on talks over defector fate.
newsitem.headline: Deng's death puts hold on talks over defector fate.

text.p: Talks on the fate of a senior North Korean defector marooned in Seoul's Beijing mission have been put on hold by the death of China's paramount leader Deng Xiaoping, Seoul officials said on Thursday.

"China and South Korea share the same Asian tradition and you just don't want to disturb mourning people," a Seoul foreign ministry official told Reuters when asked about developments over defector Hwang Jang-yop.
"We will refrain from raising Hwang's issue with Chinese officials for the time being," said the official, who asked not to be identified.
He said a short-term delay in the talks over Hwang would not seriously affect his fate since his departure from Beijing was not imminent.

Hwang, ranked 24th in Pyongyang's hierarchy, arrived at South Korea's consular office in Beijing with an aide on February 12, forcing China to tread a line between traditional ally North Korea and new business partner South Korea.

"Delay in our negotiations over Hwang appears inevitable but that progress could be speeded up after Deng's funeral," the official said. China on Thursday declared six days of moruning for Deng, who died late on Wednesday.

Another ministry official said Hwang had videotaped confirmation of his defection and this had been passed to the Chinese government before signs emerged that North Korea might be ready to give up its fight to get Hwang back.

In the first indication of change, Pyongyang's Foreign Ministry said late on Monday it would dismiss Hwang if he defected. Pyongyang had earlier been adamant in its claim that Hwang, the North's top ideologue, was kidnapped by South Korea.
Seoul officials said China might have shown Hwang's videotape to North Koreans but added that there had been no significant progress in talks over Hwang.
Foreign ministry spokesman Lee Kyu-hyung denied a Japanese newspaper report that China and South Korea had agreed Hwang leave Beijing for Seoul as early as this week.
Lee said it was too early to talk about when Hwang could leave Beijing since Chinese and South Korean officials were at "an initial stage" of their discussions.
In Beijing, China announced to its people for the first time on Wednesday that Hwang had entered the embassy of South Korea in the capital, and hinted that he had defected.
The official Xinhua news agency indicated Hwang had sought refuge in Seoul's mission of his own free will.

Highlighting concern in South Korea that the defection showed serious instability in Pyongyang, South Korea's ruling party chairman Lee Hong-koo warned that Seoul must re-think its policy on reunification with the North.
"Severe food shortages and economic difficulties are driving the North Korean system to an irreversible final crisis," Lee said on Wednesday.
But a spokesman of Seoul's national unificiation ministry said on Thursday South Korea would join international efforts to help ease food shortages in the famine-striken North.

He said Seoul would send $6 million in food aid to Pyongyang in response to the World Food Programme's appeal for $41.5 million to meet North Korea's food needs. The North's chronic food shortage has been worsened by devastating floods in the past two years.
The $6 million will be in addition to $3 million which Seoul contributed to a similar WFP aid programme last year.
The United States said it would be sending an extra 10 million dollars food aid. Washington contributed $6.4 million to the U.N. body in 1996.
